subject: English
topic: Reading Comprehension II — inference, tone, title, vocabulary in context
description: RC skills: identifying main idea, author tone, inference questions, vocabulary in context, title selection, fact vs inference distinction.

questions.stem: In an RC passage the author states: 'While renewable energy has made remarkable progress, dismissing fossil fuels overnight would be naive.' The author's tone is best described as:

options.option_text: Balanced/pragmatic — acknowledges renewables' progress while cautioning against hasty fossil fuel elimination
Strongly pro-fossil fuel — the author defends fossil fuels and attacks renewable energy
Pessimistic about renewables — the author doubts renewables can ever replace fossil fuels
Sarcastic — the tone is measured and rational, not satirical or mocking (not this) instead

questions.explanation: TONE ANALYSIS: 'remarkable progress' = positive view of renewables. 'would be naive' = caution against rushing. The author is NOT anti-renewable (uses 'remarkable') nor anti-fossil (says dismissal would be naive). This is a balanced, pragmatic stance. EXAM SKILL: identify what the author affirms vs qualifies. Balanced tone = acknowledges both sides. Other tones: cynical (general distrust), optimistic (unconditional positivity), alarmist (urgent fear). PYQ: tone questions are the most commonly tested RC skill in IBPS PO/Clerk English.

questions.stem: A passage discusses how social media algorithms amplify outrage to maximise engagement, leading to polarisation. Which title best captures the central idea?

options.option_text: Outrage as a Business Model: How Algorithms Profit from Division — directly captures the engagement-outrage-polarisation link
The Benefits of Social Media for Modern Communication — ignores the critical, negative focus of the passage
History of Social Media Platforms from 2004 to Present — the passage is thematic, not historical/chronological
How to Reduce Your Screen Time Effectively — the passage is analytical, not prescriptive self-help advice

questions.explanation: TITLE SELECTION SKILL: the best title must capture the CENTRAL ARGUMENT, not a peripheral detail or misrepresent the tone. Key elements of this passage: algorithms, outrage amplification, engagement motive (business model), polarisation result. Option A captures all four elements. Option B is opposite in tone. Option C is off-topic (historical). Option D is practical self-help — irrelevant to the analytical argument. EXAM RULE: the correct title for analytical/argumentative passages almost always mirrors the cause-effect chain at the core of the argument.

questions.stem: A passage states: 'Despite India's significant strides in digital infrastructure, rural areas remain largely excluded from the benefits.' Which inference is MOST valid?

options.option_text: Digital inclusion in India is uneven, with a persistent rural-urban digital divide
India has no digital infrastructure at all — the word 'significant strides' contradicts this conclusion
Rural areas prefer to remain offline by choice rather than due to infrastructure gaps
Digital infrastructure is more advanced in India than in any other developing nation

questions.explanation: INFERENCE SKILL: valid inference = conclusion that logically follows from what the passage states, without going beyond it. PASSAGE SAYS: (1) India has made significant digital progress. (2) Rural areas remain excluded. INFERENCE A: 'uneven digital inclusion / rural-urban divide' — directly supported by both elements. INVALID INFERENCES: B contradicts 'significant strides.' C introduces an unsupported claim about preference. D introduces a comparative global claim not mentioned. EXAM RULE: the correct inference never contradicts the passage and never introduces outside information — it is the logical conclusion of what is explicitly stated.

questions.stem: In a passage, the word 'INIMICAL' appears in the sentence: 'Such policies are inimical to long-term economic growth.' In this context, 'inimical' most nearly means:

options.option_text: Harmful or hostile to — inimical (from Latin inimicus = enemy) means actively adverse or damaging to
Beneficial to — opposite meaning; 'inimical to growth' means damaging, not helping growth
Neutral toward — inimical is not neutral; it implies active opposition or harm
Unrelated to — the sentence implies a direct negative relationship, not irrelevance

questions.explanation: INIMICAL: from Latin INIMICUS (enemy). Means: HARMFUL TO, HOSTILE TO, ADVERSE TO. 'Inimical to growth' = harmful to growth/working against growth. FAMILY: enemy, enmity, inimical — all from the same root. USAGE: 'practices inimical to public health'; 'conditions inimical to democracy.' CONTEXT CLUE: the sentence criticises the policies (they harm something long-term) — this narrows the meaning to 'harmful/hostile.' PYQ: 'inimical' appears in IBPS PO RC passages; vocabulary-in-context questions require using the sentence context, not just memorised definitions.

questions.stem: A passage argues: 'Microfinance has empowered women in rural India by giving them financial agency, yet it has also burdened some with unmanageable debt cycles.' The author's primary purpose is to:

options.option_text: Present a nuanced assessment — acknowledging microfinance's empowerment potential while flagging its debt-trap risk
Advocate for abolishing microfinance — a blanket rejection is not supported; the author acknowledges the benefits too
Promote microfinance as a solution for rural poverty without qualification — this ignores the second half of the statement
Compare Indian microfinance with international models — no comparison with other countries is present in the passage

questions.explanation: PURPOSE IDENTIFICATION: look at what the author is trying to DO with the text. The sentence has TWO parts connected by 'yet': (1) positive = financial agency/empowerment. (2) negative = debt burden. The author's purpose is to give a BALANCED/NUANCED view — neither wholly endorsing nor condemning microfinance. EXAM SKILL: when a passage uses 'yet,' 'however,' 'but,' 'despite' — the author is making a two-sided argument. The purpose is assessment/evaluation, not advocacy or comparison. PYQ: author's purpose questions are tested in every IBPS PO mains English section.

questions.stem: In an RC passage about urban planning: 'The city's arterial roads, designed in the 1970s, are now choked by a volume of traffic that was inconceivable to their planners.' What does 'arterial' most likely mean in this context?

options.option_text: Main or principal — arterial roads are the main routes, like arteries carrying blood in the body
Medical or surgical — 'arterial' here is a metaphor, not a reference to human anatomy
Ancient or historical — arterial refers to function (main route), not age of the road
Narrow and congested — the congestion is caused by traffic volume, not the road's original design width

questions.explanation: ARTERIAL (roads): from ARTERY (blood vessel carrying blood from heart). Metaphorical extension: arterial road = a major road that carries the main flow of traffic, like an artery carries blood. CONTEXT CLUES: 'choked by a volume of traffic' confirms these roads are meant to carry large traffic flows (= main roads). 'Designed in the 1970s' refers to their history, not their definition. URBAN PLANNING VOCABULARY: arterial (main), collector (secondary), local (residential). PYQ: vocabulary in context from urban planning/economics passages appears in IBPS PO mains RC.

questions.stem: A passage concludes: 'It is not the absence of talent but the absence of systems that perpetuates poverty.' Which of the following best identifies the author's implied assumption?

options.option_text: Talent is evenly distributed; poverty persists because institutional and systemic support is lacking
Poor people lack the talent to escape poverty regardless of external support systems
Systems alone cannot address poverty; individual talent must also be cultivated deliberately
The author believes poverty is primarily a cultural phenomenon linked to values and attitudes

questions.explanation: IMPLIED ASSUMPTION: the unstated premise that makes the argument logically valid. The author's argument: poverty is NOT due to lack of talent; it IS due to lack of systems. ASSUMPTION required: talent is present (distributed) — otherwise saying 'absence of systems' is the cause would be incomplete. The statement implies: talent exists everywhere but systems (education, credit, infrastructure, opportunity) are absent for the poor. STRUCTURAL ARGUMENT: this is a classic 'not X but Y' construction — the assumption is that X (talent) is NOT the problem. PYQ: implied assumption questions appear in IBPS PO mains critical reasoning / RC sections.
